summary: Wanderglass is a free web tool that lets anyone enter a star name or sky coordinates to watch how that patch of sky changed over the year SPHEREx has been observing it. It finds every SPEHREx image of the spot, lines them up on one sky grid, and plays them like a flip-book. Hence, highlighting moving objects such as nearby stars and brown dwarfs. It can follow an object with known motion, co-add or subtract frames, overlay Gaia stars and bad pixels, extract a spectrum from any pixel, and guide newcomers using five famous targets. A journal lets visitors flag candidates and export them for further analysis.
details:
What Wanderglass does

  • Search of Quick targets:
    - Type a name or RA/Dec, or pick one of five targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis).
  • Blink player:
    - Every SPHEREx image of the spot, aligned and played in date order, with scrubber and speed control.
  • Follow motion:
    - Give an object's proper motion and the field slides while the object stays pinned at the crosshair.
  • Wavelength window:
    - Each frame samples a different colour, so you can compare only frames of matching wavelength.
  • Co-add & Difference views:
    - Averaging frames reveals faint sources; late-minus-early shows movers as white/black pairs.
  • Overlays:
    - Bad pixels (cosmic rays, saturation) in red; Gaia DR3 stars as circles that follow each star's own motion.
  • Spectrum at any pixel:
    - Brightness versus wavelength, one point per frame.
  • Guided tour, stargazer's journal, red-light mode:
    - A five-stop tour with what to look for; flag a view, add a note, export CSV.
    - A red theme that protects night vision at the eyepiece.
  • Shareable links:
    - The address bar holds the whole view, so a link reopens it.

How does Wanderglass work

  1. Ask NASA/IPAC IRSA which SPHEREx images cover the position (TAP query).
  2. Download a small cutout of each image through IRSA's cutout service.
  3. Mask bad pixels, then resample every cutout onto one north-up sky grid using each image's own coordinate solution, so stars stay put.
  4. Apply proper motion (looked up from SIMBAD or typed in) to centre the grid where the object is during the survey, or to follow it frame by frame.
  5. Serve the aligned frames to a single web page that plays, stacks, subtracts and plots them.

Benefits & Unique Features

  • Built for everyone:
    - One page, plain language, a guided tour, and links that reopen any view.
  • Follow motion plus wavelength matching:
    - Addresses the two things that make SPHEREx blinking tricky: objects move, and every frame is a different colour.
  • Careful engineering:
    - Automated tests for alignment, downloads, the server, overlays and spectrum extraction, a minimal set of dependencies pinned by hash and checked for known vulnerabilities, inputs validated, patient retries, time limits, saved answers and plain-language errors when the archive is slow or down.
  • Personality:
    - A red-light mode and a stargazer's journal, built by someone who actually watches the sky.

Results so far

(Based on recommended testing data)

  • Alignment: on real SPHEREx frames of the WISE 0855 field, all 43 frames agree to within about 0.1 pixel (median).
  • Epsilon Indi B: with its proper motion applied, the bright source stays pinned at the crosshair while background stars drift.
  • Barnard's Star: with no motion applied, it appears about 44 pixels (about 4.5 arcminutes) north of its year-2000 position, matching its known 10.3 arcseconds per year over 26 years.
  • WISE 0855: a faint source consistent with the brown dwarf appears at the predicted position in the co-add with motion tracking.
  • RW Aurigae and R Draconis: very bright, so their cores saturate at 4.4 to 5.0 µm, the tool masks them and says so.

Limitations

  • It depends on IRSA being available however, it saves answers so previously loaded targets still work.
  • Spectra are approximate, meaning a 3x3-pixel aperture, local background, no aperture correction, and a straight-line model of wavelength across each tiny cutout.
  • The bad-pixel list follows a documented default, not every possible flag.
  • It currently runs from a local server but public hosting with rate limiting is the next step.
  • It is only a beginner's viewing tool, not a discovery claim.

Future Plans

Public hosting, light curves for variable stars, colour images from several detector bands, sharing a candidate list between users, an exact per-pixel wavelength lookup, and an automated candidate scoring.

Use of SI (declaration)

I used Claude (an AI assistant from Anthropic) as a coding and writing partner. Claude helped design the architecture, wrote and tested the Python server and the web page, and drafted documentation. I chose the project, set the direction and features, ran everything against real SPHEREx data, checked the results, and decided what to claim. I reviewed AI-written text and code, and the scientific statements are cross-checked against the sources declared in References.
